techniques.name: Contrastive Explanation Method
techniques.description: The Contrastive Explanation Method (CEM) explains one prediction of a classifier, such as a neural network, by describing what is present and what is absent in the input. A pertinent positive is the smallest set of features already present that is enough for the model to give the same prediction. A pertinent negative is the smallest set of features not currently present that would change the prediction to a different class if they were added. CEM finds both by solving an optimisation problem that searches for the smallest change to the input, and it can use an autoencoder (a model trained to reconstruct realistic inputs) to keep the changed inputs realistic. An explanation reads like 'this digit is a 3 because these strokes are present and because a short bar at the top is absent', since adding that bar would make it a 5.

example_use_cases.description: A procurement team uses a neural-network model that rates invoices as low, medium or high risk. For a high-risk invoice, the pertinent positives are the few triggered events that are enough for that rating, such as a large amount and a vendor with only a PO box. The pertinent negatives are events that did not occur but would lower the rating if they had, such as the vendor being registered. Reviewers check both before blocking payment.

A clinician reviews a decision-support model that suggests flu rather than pneumonia for a patient. The pertinent positives are the findings that are enough for that suggestion, such as cough, cold and fever. The pertinent negatives are findings that are absent but would move the suggestion to pneumonia if present, such as sputum and chills. The clinician compares both with their own reasoning to judge whether the model weighs the right findings.

A council uses a model to screen applications for housing support. When an application is declined, the pertinent negatives show which missing items, such as proof of tenancy, would have changed the outcome if present. A caseworker checks that each item is something the applicant can provide, then includes it in the decision notice.

limitations.description: Each explanation needs its own optimisation run for a single instance, so explaining many decisions is slow. Models whose gradients cannot be accessed need numerical gradient estimates, which slows it further.

Several settings shape the result, including how strongly the search favours small changes, how confident the model must be in the new class, and whether an autoencoder is used. Different settings can give different pertinent positives and negatives for the same instance, so they need checking with someone who knows the domain.

Changed inputs can be unrealistic. Without an autoencoder trained on good-quality data, a pertinent negative may describe an input that could never occur, so the explanation says little about real cases. Where data is scarce or poor, a good autoencoder may not be possible.

Absence has to be defined by the user. CEM adds or removes features relative to a value that stands for no signal, such as a blank pixel, and a poor choice gives meaningless pertinent negatives. This is natural for images and binary indicators, and needs domain judgement for continuous or categorical tabular data.

A pertinent negative is the smallest change the model responds to, not advice a person can act on. It may involve a feature that cannot be changed, such as age, and nothing in the method checks that the change is feasible. It is most useful when the two classes are close; if they are very different, there can be too many pertinent negatives to read.

resources.title: Explanations based on the Missing: Towards Contrastive Explanations with Pertinent Negatives
resources.abstract: In this paper we propose a novel method that provides contrastive explanations justifying the classification of an input by a black box classifier such as a deep neural network. Given an input we find what should be %necessarily and minimally and sufficiently present (viz. important object pixels in an image) to justify its classification and analogously what should be minimally and necessarily \emph{absent} (viz. certain background pixels). We argue that such explanations are natural for humans and are used commonly in domains such as health care and criminology. What is minimally but critically \emph{absent} is an important part of an explanation, which to the best of our knowledge, has not been explicitly identified by current explanation methods that explain predictions of neural networks. We validate our approach on three real datasets obtained from diverse domains; namely, a handwritten digits dataset MNIST, a large procurement fraud dataset and a brain activity strength dataset. In all three cases, we witness the power of our approach in generating precise explanations that are also easy for human experts to understand and evaluate.

resources.title: Contrastive Explanations Method (CEM) applied to MNIST — Alibi Explain
Understanding How CNNs Recognize Facial Expressions: A Case Study with LIME and CEM
resources.abstract: Recognizing facial expressions has been a persistent goal in the scientific community. Since the rise of artificial intelligence, convolutional neural networks (CNN) have become popular to recognize facial expressions, as images can be directly used as input. Current CNN models can achieve high recognition rates, but they give no clue about their reasoning process. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been developed as a means to help to interpret the results obtained by machine learning models. When dealing with images, one of the most-used XAI techniques is LIME. LIME highlights the areas of the image that contribute to a classification. As an alternative to LIME, the CEM method appeared, providing explanations in a way that is natural for human classification: besides highlighting what is sufficient to justify a classification, it also identifies what should be absent to maintain it and to distinguish it from another classification. This study presents the results of comparing LIME and CEM applied over complex images such as facial expression images. While CEM could be used to explain the results on images described with a reduced number of features, LIME would be the method of choice when dealing with images described with a huge number of features.

sample_claims.text: For the invoices the risk model rates high, compliance reviewers judge that the pertinent positives are sufficient grounds for the rating and the pertinent negatives are events that would lower it.
For each flagged patient record, the pertinent positives and negatives match the findings clinicians use to tell the model's diagnosis from the nearest alternative.
On the instances tested, keeping only the pertinent positive leaves the model's prediction unchanged, and adding the pertinent negative changes it to a different class.
Each applicant declined for credit is told which absent factors, if present, would have changed the model's decision, and a reviewer has confirmed that each is something the applicant could change.
Caseworkers can tell an applicant which missing information, if provided, would change the eligibility model's outcome for that application.

techniques.name: Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards
techniques.description: Human-in-the-loop safeguards hold an AI system's output at a checkpoint until a trained person has reviewed it. Designers set the rules that send a case to review, such as low model confidence (the system's own estimate of how likely it is to be right), a high-stakes outcome or a request to appeal. Some schemes also review a random sample of routine cases to audit the rest. The reviewer approves, changes or rejects the output, and the record of each review shows how often people overrode the system. Review protects only where reviewers keep using independent judgement, so the design also has to guard against over-trust and fatigue.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing mandatory human physician review for any medical AI diagnostic recommendation before treatment decisions are made, especially for complex cases or when the system confidence is below established thresholds, ensuring patient safety through expert oversight.

Requiring human review of automated loan approval decisions when applicants request explanations or appeal rejections, allowing human underwriters to provide clear reasoning and ensure customers understand the decision-making process behind their application outcomes.

A recruitment agency requires a named recruiter to confirm or reverse every automated rejection before it is sent, and logs the decision and the reason. The agency's governance board reviews the override rate each quarter to see whether the screening tool and its reviewers are working as intended.

limitations.description: Review capacity sets a ceiling. As volume rises, cases queue, decisions are delayed and time-sensitive uses become impractical, so the escalation rules must be tuned to what the available trained reviewers can handle.
Reviewers tire and drift. Attention and consistency fall over a long shift or a run of similar cases, so two reviewers, or one reviewer at different times, may decide the same case differently.

Automation bias. People tend to accept a system's recommendation, particularly under time pressure, so review can become a rubber stamp. A very high approval rate with almost no overrides may signal this rather than a good system.

The escalation rules decide what a human ever sees. A confidently wrong output passes without review when only low-confidence cases are escalated, so reviewing a random sample of routine cases is needed to find these errors.

Human review does not reliably improve decisions. A meta-analysis of 106 experiments found human-AI combinations performed worse on average than the better of human or AI alone, with losses in decision-making tasks. The effect of a checkpoint should be tested, not assumed.

resources.title: Improving the Applicability of AI for Psychiatric Applications through Human-in-the-loop Methodologies
resources.abstract: Objectives Machine learning (ML) and natural language processing have great potential to improve efficiency and accuracy in diagnosis, treatment recommendations, predictive interventions, and scarce resource allocation within psychiatry. Researchers often conceptualize such an approach as operating in isolation without much need for human involvement, yet it remains crucial to harness human-in-the-loop practices when developing and implementing such techniques as their absence may be catastrophic. We advocate for building ML-based technologies that collaborate with experts within psychiatry in all stages of implementation and use to increase model performance while simultaneously increasing the practicality, robustness, and reliability of the process. Methods We showcase pitfalls of the traditional ML framework and explain how it can be improved with human-in-the-loop techniques. Specifically, we applied active learning strategies to the automatic scoring of a story recall task and compared the results to a traditional approach. Results Human-in-the-loop methodologies supplied a greater understanding of where the model was least confident or had knowledge gaps during training. As compared to the traditional framework, less than half of the training data were needed to reach a given accuracy. Conclusions Human-in-the-loop ML is an approach to data collection and model creation that harnesses active learning to select the most critical data needed to increase a model’s accuracy and generalizability more efficiently than classic random sampling would otherwise allow. Such techniques may additionally operate as safeguards from spurious predictions and can aid in decreasing disparities that artificial intelligence systems otherwise propagate.

resources.title: A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation
resources.abstract: Technical developments in computer hardware and software now make it possible to introduce automation into virtually all aspects of human-machine systems. Given these technical capabilities, which system functions should be automated and to what extent? We outline a model for types and levels of automation that provides a framework and an objective basis for making such choices. Appropriate selection is important because automation does not merely supplant but changes human activity and can impose new coordination demands on the human operator. We propose that automation can be applied to four broad classes of functions: 1) information acquisition; 2) information analysis; 3) decision and action selection; and 4) action implementation. Within each of these types, automation can be applied across a continuum of levels from low to high, i.e., from fully manual to fully automatic. A particular system can involve automation of all four types at different levels. The human performance consequences of particular types and levels of automation constitute primary evaluative criteria for automation design using our model. Secondary evaluative criteria include automation reliability and the costs of decision/action consequences, among others. Examples of recommended types and levels of automation are provided to illustrate the application of the model to automation design.

resources.title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: A systematic review and meta-analysis
resources.abstract: Inspired by the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) to augment humans, researchers have studied human–AI systems involving different tasks, systems and populations. Despite such a large body of work, we lack a broad conceptual understanding of when combinations of humans and AI are better than either alone. Here we addressed this question by conducting a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of 106 experimental studies reporting 370 effect sizes. We searched an interdisciplinary set of databases (the Association for Computing Machinery Digital Library, the Web of Science and the Association for Information Systems eLibrary) for studies published between 1 January 2020 and 30 June 2023. Each study was required to include an original human-participants experiment that evaluated the performance of humans alone, AI alone and human–AI combinations. First, we found that, on average, human–AI combinations performed significantly worse than the best of humans or AI alone (Hedges’ g = −0.23; 95% confidence interval, −0.39 to −0.07). Second, we found performance losses in tasks that involved making decisions and significantly greater gains in tasks that involved creating content. Finally, when humans outperformed AI alone, we found performance gains in the combination, but when AI outperformed humans alone, we found losses. Limitations of the evidence assessed here include possible publication bias and variations in the study designs analysed. Overall, these findings highlight the heterogeneity of the effects of human–AI collaboration and point to promising avenues for improving human–AI systems.

resources.title: Article 14: Human Oversight | EU Artificial Intelligence Act
Human-in-the-loop machine learning: a state of the art
resources.abstract: Researchers are defining new types of interactions between humans and machine learning algorithms generically called human-in-the-loop machine learning. Depending on who is in control of the learning process, we can identify: active learning, in which the system remains in control; interactive machine learning, in which there is a closer interaction between users and learning systems; and machine teaching, where human domain experts have control over the learning process. Aside from control, humans can also be involved in the learning process in other ways. In curriculum learning human domain experts try to impose some structure on the examples presented to improve the learning; in explainable AI the focus is on the ability of the model to explain to humans why a given solution was chosen. This collaboration between AI models and humans should not be limited only to the learning process; if we go further, we can see other terms that arise such as Usable and Useful AI. In this paper we review the state of the art of the techniques involved in the new forms of relationship between humans and ML algorithms. Our contribution is not merely listing the different approaches, but to provide definitions clarifying confusing, varied and sometimes contradictory terms; to elucidate and determine the boundaries between the different methods; and to correlate all the techniques searching for the connections and influences between them.

techniques.name: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations
techniques.description: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) explains one decision of a classifier by generating several altered versions of the input, called counterfactuals, each changed just enough that the model would have given the other outcome, and chosen to differ from one another so that a person sees several distinct ways the result could have been different. Where the contrastive explanation method returns, for one input, a minimal set of features that must be present and a minimal set that must stay absent, DiCE returns several complete alternative inputs at once, within limits the user sets on which features may change and over what range. In the original method all the counterfactuals are optimised together by gradient descent on a loss with three parts: a hinge loss that pushes each across the model's decision threshold, a distance term (each continuous feature's change divided by its median absolute deviation in the training data, plus the share of categorical features changed) that keeps each close to the original, and a diversity term, the determinant of a similarity matrix between them, that rewards them for differing. Afterwards, small changes are reset to their original values for as long as the counterfactual still gets the other outcome, to make it sparser, and counterfactuals that break causal rules supplied by the user, such as gaining a degree without growing older, can be filtered out. The method as published needs a differentiable model such as a neural network; the reference library adds random-sampling, genetic-algorithm and nearest-training-example searches that need only the model's predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A credit-risk validation team at a lender generates five counterfactuals for each of 500 sampled refused applications with every feature free to change, to see what the model treats as enough for approval. Counterfactuals that reach approval by changing only the postcode, or another likely proxy for a protected characteristic, are logged as findings and passed to the fairness testing team.

A hospital team piloting a classifier that places patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in low, moderate or high cardiovascular risk generates counterfactuals restricted to modifiable factors such as blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking. Clinicians check whether the changes the model links to a lower risk category agree with clinical knowledge before the tool is shown to patients.

A consumer lender puts up to three counterfactuals in each refusal letter, generated against the model version that made the decision and limited to features the applicant can change (income, balances, loan amount and term), each shown as an application that would have been approved. Before rollout it tests a draft letter with applicants, checking that they can name a change that would have worked and understand that the options are not a promise of approval if they reapply.

limitations.description: A counterfactual is only valid for the model version that produced it. The method assumes the model does not change, and after retraining a previously suggested change can stop flipping the decision, so a person who acts on it may still be refused. Counterfactuals shown to people should be dated, tied to a model version and re-checked whenever the model is updated.

Feasibility depends on constraints the user supplies. Without them, counterfactuals can change attributes a person cannot change, such as race or sex, or propose impossible combinations: in the original experiments over a third of the counterfactuals that changed education were infeasible, most raising the degree without raising age. Causal rules can only be applied afterwards, as a filter.

The set returned is not unique. It depends on the weights on distance and diversity, per-feature weights, the number requested and random starting points, and with the library's random-sampling method a different seed gives a different set. The authors note that showing people counterfactuals produced with different settings is a problem, so fix and record settings and seeds.

Distance is measured feature by feature (scaled change for numbers, changed or not for categories), so it ignores how features move together, treats every category change as equally hard, and can place counterfactuals where there is little real data. In a study of 9,613 patient records, DiCE's counterfactuals were closer and sparser but less plausible than those of a sampling-based alternative.

The original paper tests no people. Its stand-in for understanding, a nearest-neighbour model trained on the counterfactuals, is in the authors' words a best case of rational extrapolation, and they leave a behavioural study and the cost of choosing among more options to future work. A counterfactual also does not say which features must stay as they are, so a person who raises income by changing job may still be refused. Test the wording with recipients before relying on it.

techniques.name: Actionable Recourse Audit
techniques.description: An actionable recourse audit checks whether the people a linear classifier refuses, for example for a loan, a job interview or a public service, could change that decision through actions open to them, and how much they would have to change. The auditor first writes an action set saying which features can change and how: immutable features such as age stay fixed, features such as education level can only rise, and each changeable feature gets bounds and a grid of realistic values. Then, for each refused person in a sample drawn from the population the model will serve, an integer programming solver (optimisation software that searches discrete choices exactly) looks through the permitted actions for the cheapest change that flips the decision, measuring cost as the largest shift, in population percentiles, that the change makes to any one feature, and either returns that action or proves that none exists, which a search that simply fails to find a counterfactual cannot do. The audit reports the share of refused people who have recourse and the distribution of its cost, which can be compared across candidate models or broken down by group, and the same solver can list a refused person's cheapest alternative changes (a 'flipset') for a decision notice. Unlike the Contrastive Explanation Method, which explains one prediction through features that must be present or absent, or Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE), which searches any model for several alternative inputs that would change one decision, the audit works only on linear models but certifies whether any permitted action exists and summarises the answer across a population.

example_use_cases.description: Before launching a linear model that ranks applications to a housing support scheme, a local authority's analytics team audits recourse on last year's applicants, with age and household size fixed. Its report to the scheme's oversight board gives the share of refused applicants who could qualify through changes the scheme expects, such as completing a tenancy course, and how large those changes are, so the board can decide whether to approve the model.

A credit card issuer generates a flipset for each applicant its linear scorecard declines and puts the two cheapest items in the decline letter, for example reducing current debt to a stated amount, together with the other scored features the applicant should keep unchanged, so that following the stated actions would change the decision under the current model.

A lender's model risk committee is shown recourse audits for candidate credit models of almost equal accuracy. It rejects the most accurate, under which some refused applicants had no feasible action because of an 'ever defaulted' feature, adopts a variant that uses recent defaults only, and has the audit re-run each quarter on new applicants, watching younger applicants, who were scarce in the training data.

An employer's analytics team audits its linear screening model for interview invitations and compares the cost of recourse for refused women and men with similar predicted scores. Sex is not a model input, but the cost can still differ by sex. Refused candidates' true suitability is never observed, so the team cannot also match on outcome as the originating study did, and reports any gap with that caveat to its fairness review panel, which decides whether the features need revising.

limitations.description: The proof that no action exists depends on the model being linear, such as logistic regression, a linear support vector machine or a rule set that can be written in linear form. For tree ensembles or neural networks, a local linear approximation can still suggest actions, which then have to be checked on the real model, but a failure to find one proves nothing, so the share of refused people without recourse is no longer a certified figure.

Every conclusion rests on the action set and cost the auditor chooses. Bounds that are too tight make people appear to lack recourse; loose bounds let a model 'provide' recourse only through drastic changes, which shows only as high cost; and the default cost treats a one-percentile change as equally hard in every feature unless someone who knows the domain sets how much harder some changes are.

The search treats features as changing independently unless the auditor adds constraints. Real actions have knock-on effects: raising income can also raise savings, so a listed action may cost more than needed, or may not change the decision once its effects on other features are counted, as Karimi, Schölkopf and Valera showed for recourse methods that ignore causal relations between features.

Recourse is defined for a fixed model. After retraining, an action given in an earlier notice may no longer change the decision, so the audit has to be re-run after each update. An action that changes the prediction need not change the real outcome either: showing a refused applicant how to be approved can lead them into credit they cannot repay.

A flipset lists only the features to change, so a person who also changes an undisclosed feature may still be refused unless the notice says what must stay the same. The originating paper builds flipsets from public credit datasets and does not test whether refused people understand them or can act on them. Owners may also resist publishing flipsets, because many of them together can let others reconstruct the model.
